summary:
Atacama Region stands under Chile's national framework. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults change registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

Discrimination and hate-crime law covers the visitor directly. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children, in place since 2006.

Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, records no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information, so the region is assessed at the national score and a visitor's expectations are set by national law rather than regional ordinance. The same dossier records the 2025-26 rollback in which the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombud for children.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Documented abuse is rising in Atacama. Movilh's XXIV annual report, published March 2026, places the region at 1.83% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 7.69%. Nationally the report counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest in 24 years; only two regions fell while the other 14 rose. The report reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate.

Transphobic violence remains documented at national level. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention and health care carry specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee overseeing implementation including access rules for trans visitors. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.
tangentialFactors:
Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, recommending elimination of the Gender Identity Support Program, restriction of minors' progressive autonomy, a ban on hormonal treatment for minors and repeal of the circular protecting gender identity in schools. The recommendation does not change the law a visitor is subject to.

Movilh records two region-level positives: the Municipality of Atacama convened the commune's first Pride march, and Atacama and Puerto Varas became the first regions to hold Pride marches during 2025, expanding the movement's territorial visibility. In the same national table only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) recorded year-on-year falls in documented abuse.
localsOnly:
Residents face the court route for minors: applicants aged 14 to 18 must petition the family court with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the statute's under-14 exclusion remains the general rule despite the Constitutional Court's single-case ruling of 9 April 2025.

Care and support programmes are funded unevenly. The public health system has financed sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular requires care centres to register transgender patients by social name. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Detainees are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on gender identity, which provides placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations under a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives, including rules on visits by trans people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Atacama-specific incident, arrest, prosecution or enforcement finding is sourced; the region's only quantified indicator is Movilh's 1.83% share of nationally documented abuse cases for 2025, and Movilh figures are NGO documentation rather than official crime statistics.

Movilh's 2024 comparison baseline is unresolved: the 2024 share used to derive the 7.69% regional rise is not reproduced in the 2025 edition, so the percentage change cannot be checked against the published table.

Whether the Ministry of Health-run support programme operates in Atacama's own medical centres, and whether Crece con Orgullo has a local service point, is not sourced.

Outright International's dossier provides no division-level breakdown for Chile, so no region-specific legal or enforcement assessment can be drawn from it.
